passage: Last Wednesday I only went to Room 12 to collect the hall key, but I stayed to watch the annual-day committee. Arnab wrote the numbers 1 to 30 on the board and said, "No comments until we reach thirty." Ideas flew: a retro night, a monsoon carnival, an upside-down day. Someone said, "That's silly." Arnab just tapped the board and said, "Thirty first." When the board was full, they talked. Some ideas merged. Hands went up for the vote, and three were left: retro night, carnival, school in space. A boy near the window, who I'd never heard speak at a meeting, offered the last one, and it made the final three. I can't say what he felt, but he was smiling. - Kiran

qa.q: How many ideas did the committee list before discussing?
qa.a: The committee listed thirty ideas before discussing.

qa.q: What does Arnab's calm tapping of the board suggest, and how sure can Kiran be?
qa.a: Arnab seems calm and determined to keep ideas flowing without judgement, though Kiran can only guess from what was seen.

qa.q: What could the committee do next if all three finalists turn out too costly, and why?
qa.a: They could check cost and space for each and merge parts of the ideas, because everyone has already contributed and a workable choice can still be shaped.

qa.q: What was it like for the boy near the window when his idea was not judged?
qa.a: The boy probably felt safe enough to speak and proud when his idea reached the final three, since the rule stopped anyone from dismissing it. 😊

grounding: The committee lists thirty theme ideas without judging, then narrows to three by discussion and votes, so everyone contributes before converging on a workable choice.

passage: Zeynep drew a table on a big sheet in the corridor of her school in Istanbul: Decoration, Music, Food, Invitations. Beside each, one name and a date. Decoration: Aiko, by Thursday. Music: Emre, playlist by Friday morning. Food: Lucas, list to the teacher by Wednesday. Invitations: Zeynep herself, printed by Tuesday. "Not 'the team,'" she said, capping her marker. "One name each." Aiko grinned. "So if the paper lanterns fail, it's my fault." "And if they work?" "Then it's my glory." On Wednesday Lucas handed in the food list, and on Thursday Aiko arrived with two boxes of lanterns. Only the music slipped by a day, and Zeynep knew exactly whom to ask.

qa.q: Who was responsible for decoration and by when?
qa.a: Aiko was responsible for decoration, by Thursday.

qa.q: How does Aiko feel about owning the lanterns?
qa.a: Aiko feels cheerful and willing to take responsibility, joking that failure would be Aiko's fault and success Aiko's glory.

qa.q: What could Zeynep add to the plan if a task slips, and why?
qa.a: Zeynep could add a short check-in a day before each date, because an early reminder catches slips while there is still time to fix them.

qa.q: How might Emre see having a named task?
qa.a: Emre knows exactly what is expected and by when, so a slip is Emre's to fix and no one else is left guessing.

grounding: Tasks are split into decoration, music, food and invitations, each assigned to one named person with a date, so nothing depends on everyone thinking someone else will do it.

subtype: Approach: last-minute leaving everything to the day [Pitfall]
passage: Note, Class 9 farewell, Friday. Bhavna and Sharmila had two weeks, and they left sound, seating and the projector to the morning of the event. When I asked, they said, "It will work out." At two o'clock the microphone hummed and cut out, and thirty chairs were missing because another class had taken them. Parents stood at the back for the first twenty minutes, and two left early. Sharmila said, "We thought it would just work." Bhavna cried in the corridor. What I did: sent for chairs from the staff room, borrowed a speaker from the music room, and sat with both girls on Monday. I asked them to write what they would do differently and a checklist to hand to next year's organisers.

qa.q: What went wrong at two o'clock?
qa.a: The microphone hummed and cut out, and thirty chairs were missing.

qa.q: What might Sharmila and Bhavna be feeling after the event?
qa.a: They likely feel embarrassed and upset, shown by the admission 'We thought it would just work' and the crying in the corridor.

qa.q: What could the organisers have done earlier, and why?
qa.a: They could have tested the sound and counted the chairs a day before, because problems found early are easier to fix.

qa.q: How might the parents at the back have experienced the first twenty minutes?
qa.a: The parents were probably uncomfortable and disappointed, standing without seats and hearing poor sound, and two left early.

grounding: Assuming things will work out, the organisers wait until the final day to arrange sound and seating, and equipment problems and missing chairs cause chaos and disappoint the guests.

passage: The science-fair team met in the lab on Monday while I stacked chairs. Vishal put the marker down and said, "Imagine it's the day, and it went badly. Why?" Nobody wanted to say it, so Vishal wrote the first one himself: "Rain." Then, one after another: no microphone, volunteers don't show, the chief guest can't find the room. Vishal wrote each on the board. Beside each, a fix: a tarpaulin canopy, a spare speaker, two extra helpers with badges, signs at the gate. I don't know if Vishal is superstitious or just careful, but Vishal looked more relaxed once the board was full. - Maria

qa.q: What was the first cause of a bad day that Vishal wrote on the board?
qa.a: Vishal wrote 'Rain' first.

qa.q: How did Vishal seem to feel once the board was full, and how sure can Maria be?
qa.a: Vishal seemed more relaxed and reassured, though Maria admits not knowing whether it came from being superstitious or careful.

qa.q: What else could the team plan for, and why?
qa.a: They could plan for a lost key or a power cut, because the same exercise of naming a failure then fixing it works for any risk.

qa.q: How might the volunteers see the list of bad outcomes?
qa.a: Some may feel uneasy at first, since nobody wanted to say them, but seeing a fix beside each likely makes them feel prepared.

grounding: The team imagines the event has gone badly and lists causes such as rain, no microphone or too few volunteers, then plans a tent, a backup speaker and extra helpers.

passage:
Monday: Sachin and Farida took a one-page plan for the Saturday farewell party to their class teacher: 3 to 6 pm in the school hall. The teacher asked about supervision, the end time and travel home, and said the principal must approve too.

Wednesday: The principal signed. Farida wrote the parents' note with the time, the place, the end time of six, and a request to say who would collect each child. Sachin gathered the signed slips: twenty-eight of thirty-two.

Saturday: Two teachers sat at the back of the hall. At six, Farida read out the pick-up list at the gate, and each child left with someone on it. There was music and cake, and nothing else. Sachin was tired but pleased.

qa.q: How many signed slips did Sachin collect?
qa.a: Sachin collected twenty-eight of thirty-two signed slips.

qa.q: How did Sachin feel at the end of the party?
qa.a: Sachin felt tired but pleased, since the party ran safely to the agreed time.

qa.q: What could the organisers do about the four missing slips, and why?
qa.a: They could follow up with those four families before Saturday, because a child without a signed slip and a pick-up person should not be at risk.

qa.q: How might a parent see the pick-up request in the note?
qa.a: A parent likely feels reassured, since the note gives the end time, the place and a clear plan for getting the child home safely.

grounding: The organisers ask the teacher and parents for permission, agree an end time, keep the venue supervised, arrange safe travel home and avoid anything that could put guests at risk.

passage: Esther redrew the decoration plan for the school's Harvest Day for the sixth time on Tuesday. The ribbons had gone from gold to teal and back to gold, and the schedule now lived on five different sheets. Nkechi, in charge of tables, waited on the steps with the rest of the team for a task. "Is this final?" Nkechi asked. "Not yet," said Esther, rubbing her eyes. Week by week the team shrank: seven volunteers, then five, then three. On the day, the stage was beautifully draped, and only three people were left to serve two hundred guests. Nkechi kept the tables going and thought about all those hours, and how little the guests noticed the ribbons.

qa.q: How many times did Esther redraw the decoration plan?
qa.a: Esther redrew it for the sixth time.

qa.q: What is Nkechi feeling while waiting on the steps?
qa.a: Nkechi feels frustrated and restless, waiting for a task while the plan keeps changing.

qa.q: What could Esther do instead of redrawing again, and why?
qa.a: Esther could fix the plan, give each volunteer a task and a date, and stop polishing, because the extra changes add little while the team's energy drains.

qa.q: How might the other volunteers see Esther's changes?
qa.a: They probably feel worn out and unneeded, since they wait for tasks that never settle, which is why the team shrank from seven to three.

grounding: The head organiser redesigns the decoration plan six times and rewrites schedules, wearing out the team, and the polish adds little while volunteers lose interest before the day.

passage:
Hi Charu,

Since you missed yesterday's run-through, here is what happened. We did the whole programme with a stopwatch: welcome, dance, skit, thank-you speech. The move from the skit to the dance took almost two minutes because nobody knew who shifted the chairs. We fixed it by naming two people. Then we tested the speakers, and one would not work: the cable was missing. Somebody found a spare in the music room. Better yesterday than tomorrow at five with a hall full of guests. Tomorrow: sound check at four. Please bring your final script and come ten minutes early so we can practise your entrance once more.

Farhan

qa.q: What was missing when the group tested the speakers?
qa.a: A cable was missing.

qa.q: How does Farhan feel about finding the problems in the run-through?
qa.a: Farhan feels relieved, saying it is better to find them yesterday than in front of guests tomorrow at five.

qa.q: What could the group add to tomorrow's plan, and why?
qa.a: They could keep the spare cable next to the speakers and check it at the sound check, because a spare only helps if it is easy to reach.

qa.q: How might Charu feel on reading the email?
qa.a: Charu may feel a little left out for missing the run-through, but also reassured that the issues were solved and the entrance can still be practised.

grounding: A day before, the group walks through the whole programme with timing, tests the speakers and practises transitions, catching a missing cable while fixing is still easy.

subtype: Approach: adapting when things go wrong on the day [Revision]
passage: At six the hall in Ghent was full and the chief guest's chair was empty. Soo-ah, the stage manager, whispered, "The guest is stuck on the ring road." Tomas thought fast. The choir was scheduled after the speech, but they were already waiting in the wings. "Choir first," he said. "Then the guitar duo, then the speech when the guest arrives." Soo-ah rewrote the running order in ten seconds and told the presenter. The audience clapped through two songs, and when the guest slipped in at twenty to seven, the speech was next. Afterwards the team sat on the edge of the stage. "A twenty-minute buffer would have helped," said Soo-ah. Tomas wrote it on the checklist for next year.

qa.q: What was Tomas's first change to the running order?
qa.a: Tomas moved the choir first, before the guitar duo and the speech.

qa.q: How does Tomas seem to feel when the chief guest is late, and what shows it?
qa.a: Tomas seems calm under pressure, since he thinks fast and gives a clear new order without panic.

qa.q: What could the team add next year to avoid the problem, and why?
qa.a: They could build in a twenty-minute buffer near the start, because a delayed guest then does not force changes during the show.

qa.q: How might the audience have experienced the change?
qa.a: The audience probably noticed nothing wrong and enjoyed the music, since two songs began right away and the speech came when the guest arrived.

grounding: When the chief guest is late, the organiser moves the performance forward and adjusts the order, keeping the audience engaged, and the team later notes that a buffer would have helped.

subtype: Approach: identifying what voters actually need [Thinking]
passage: Akash sat with a blank page headed Manifesto and realised he had only "better school, better future." That meant nothing. So he decided to ask. During recess, with a notebook and one question, "What one thing would you fix?", he went from bench to bench. Canteen queues, said Aadhya; her Class 9 friends waited twenty minutes for one samosa. The football club had two working balls. The library closed at four, before club practice ended. By Friday he had ninety-one answers in tally marks, and three problems came up again and again. Akash crossed out the vague lines and wrote three: a second canteen counter, more balls, library open until five. "Now I can promise something specific," he said, "and people can check it."

qa.q: How many answers did Akash collect by Friday?
qa.a: Akash collected ninety-one answers.

qa.q: What did Akash realise about the first draft of the manifesto, and how did he feel?
qa.a: Akash realised 'better school, better future' meant nothing, and felt dissatisfied enough to go and ask classmates.

qa.q: What other approach could Akash use to check the ideas, and why?
qa.a: Akash could talk to the principal and canteen staff about what is possible, because a promise voters can check needs to be one that can be kept.

qa.q: How does Aadhya see the campaign question?
qa.a: Aadhya likely feels listened to, since a real complaint about the canteen queue was asked for and could turn into a promise.

grounding: A candidate for school captain asks classmates about canteen queues, sports equipment and library hours, and builds a platform on concrete issues instead of general promises of change.

subtype: Approach: building a small campaign team [Action]
passage: Tejas knew he could not reach every class alone. So he asked three friends from different classes: Nitin in 9B for posters, Shreya in 8A for class visits, and Imran in 10C for speeches. Every day at ten past one, in the corridor by the water cooler, the four met for ten minutes with three questions: what's done, what's stuck, who haven't we reached? On Tuesday Nitin's posters hung on every floor. On Wednesday Shreya said the Class 8s felt ignored, so Tejas added a visit. On Thursday Imran read a draft speech, and it got better after two edits. Nobody had a title. Each had a task and a time.

qa.q: Where did the four meet each day?
qa.a: They met in the corridor by the water cooler.

qa.q: What does Tejas's decision to add a visit suggest about how he feels toward the Class 8s?
qa.a: Tejas cares that the Class 8s feel included, and responds to Shreya's report with an action, not a defence.

qa.q: What could Tejas do if the ten-minute meeting shows a task is stuck, and why?
qa.a: Tejas could pair the stuck task with a second helper for one day, because sharing it lets the campaign keep moving without adding meetings.

qa.q: How might Shreya see the daily meeting?
qa.a: Shreya likely feels the voice of the Class 8s is heard, since a concern raised on Wednesday changed the plan.

grounding: The candidate recruits friends from different classes to handle posters, class visits and speeches, and meets daily for ten minutes to check progress and reach different groups of voters.
